vignette:
She is seventy-eight and has spent most of her life making order out of color, line, and shape. Even now, she still thinks of herself as a graphic designer, though she works more slowly and mostly from home. Before the storm, her days have a familiar rhythm: coffee at the kitchen table, sketches spread beside her laptop, long stretches of quiet work interrupted by calls from her husband or the mailman at the door. She has always liked precision. It gives her a sense that the world can be arranged into something understandable.

That certainty changes the night the disaster comes.

The weather has been worsening all afternoon, but at first she treats it like so many other storms she has lived through. She has seen winter gales, flooding on the news, branches down in the street. She and her husband watch the windows darken and listen to the wind gather strength around the house. By evening, the sound becomes something else entirely, a roaring pressure that seems to shake the walls from the outside in. She remembers standing in the hallway, holding her husband’s arm, trying to decide whether they should move to the basement, when the first impact hits. The noise is so sudden and violent that she cannot make sense of it at once. Later, she will describe it as if the sky itself has collided with the house.

In the hours that follow, she moves on instinct. She carries a flashlight, checks the doors, calls out to make sure her husband is still beside her. Water begins to enter in places it should not, seeping under thresholds, climbing up from the basement, finding cracks she did not know existed. The electricity fails. The dark becomes dense and complete, broken only by flashes that reveal familiar rooms transformed into something unrecognizable. She is not injured, but she feels herself becoming smaller, as though all her attention is being pulled inward to a single point of survival. She keeps thinking she needs to do something practical—document damage, protect papers, save the computer, preserve the work she has on deadline—but none of it matters in the face of the noise and rising water.

When morning comes, the house is damaged and the neighborhood looks as if it has been scraped open. Rooflines are broken, trees are down across streets, and debris is tangled in fences and porches. She is stunned by the silence after the storm, as if her body has become too alert to trust stillness. In the first days afterward, she functions mechanically. She sorts through ruined belongings, photographs the damage, fills out forms, and tries to keep up with insurance calls. Her husband becomes the steadier one, though she notices how often she is searching for him in the room, needing to see him before she can think. She tells people she is fine because it seems easier than explaining that she is not fine, not really, just busy surviving.

As the weeks pass, the disaster settles into her life in less visible ways. She cannot tolerate certain weather reports, and she begins turning the television off before the forecast ends. Windy evenings make her tense before she can name why. When rain starts against the windows, her chest tightens and she feels the old helplessness return, sharp and immediate. She sleeps lightly and wakes at the smallest sounds, listening for water, for the creak of something giving way. Sometimes she dreams of standing in her hallway in the dark, unable to move, while the house fills around her. She wakes with her heart racing and her mind briefly convinced that she is back there.

Her work changes too. Before, she could spend hours refining a layout or adjusting a font until it looked exactly right. Now she stares at the screen and loses track of what she was doing. The same concentration that once felt natural becomes difficult to summon. She rereads emails several times and still worries she has missed something. When she is frustrated, she becomes irritated with herself in a way she never used to. There is an edge of shame in this, because she has always prided herself on competence. She sees the difference in her hands when she is sketching: they tremble on some days, or she presses too hard with the pencil, as if trying to force control back into the page.

She and her husband remain close, but she notices how often she now asks where he is in the house, just to hear his voice. She avoids being alone during bad weather and keeps a lamp on in rooms she once entered without thought. The world feels less predictable than it did before, and she carries that knowledge with her even on calm days. Still, she gets up, makes breakfast, answers the phone, and opens her design files. She tells herself that the work is a way of staying connected to who she has always been. Some days it helps. Other days, it only reminds her of how much of her old ease has been interrupted by one night that has not yet finished happening inside her.
